 Official: Here’s how much minimum wage will be in Hungary in 2027 
 Hetzmann Mercédesz 
 Published: 1min ago 
 EN 
 Illustration. Photo: deposiphotos.com 
 Hungary’s minimum wage and guaranteed minimum wage for skilled workers will both increase from January 2027 after the government, employers and trade unions reached an agreement on next year’s pay rises. The new rates will mean higher gross salaries for the country’s lowest-paid workers, with planned tax relief expected to boost their take-home pay even further. 
 The agreement was announced by the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs following a meeting of the Permanent Consultation Forum of the Competitive Sector and the Government (VKF) on 19 November. The parties are expected to sign the agreement next week.
 How much will the minimum wage increase?
 Under the agreement, Hungary’s gross monthly minimum wage will rise by 7.5%, from its current level to HUF 347,000 (approximately EUR 930).
 The guaranteed minimum wage, which applies to jobs requiring at least secondary-level qualifications or vocational training, will increase by 6.1% to HUF 396,000 (approximately EUR 1,060) per month.
 The government says that, when combined with the planned tax credit, the increases could result in considerably higher net salaries for employees who are not eligible for other personal income tax allowances.
 For these workers, the net minimum wage could rise by 17.2%, or almost HUF 37,000 per month. Those earning the guaranteed minimum wage could see their take-home pay increase by 13.3%, equivalent to around HUF 33,000 monthly.
 The government argues that the arrangement strikes a balance between improving employees’ incomes and ensuring that businesses, particularly those in a more vulnerable financial position, can afford the higher wage costs.
 Employers warn that businesses must be able to afford the increases
 The agreement followed negotiations between the government, employers and employee representatives. According to the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs, the parties initially held significantly different positions but managed to reach a compromise after detailed discussions.
 The National Association of Employers and Manufacturers (MGYOSZ) described the deal as a significant commitment on the part of employers, warning that improving economic conditions would be necessary to implement it without major difficulties.
 “The parties could agree on the scale of the wage increase, but its funding cannot be decided at the negotiating table. Businesses have to generate the necessary resources on the market,” said Ákos Kalmár , a member of the MGYOSZ presidency.
 The organisation also noted that different considerations influenced the two wage rates. When setting the minimum wage, negotiators had to consider both the economic capacity of businesses and the financial situation of the lowest-paid employees. For the guaranteed minimum wage, employers’ ability to bear additional costs and labour market conditions carried greater weight.
 The final stage of negotiations reportedly involved lengthy and heated discussions over the guaranteed minimum wage. Employers and employee representatives also proposed a general 5% wage increase for the competitive sector.
 Further wage negotiations planned for 2027
 The government said the previous three-year wage agreement had been reviewed in light of changing macroeconomic conditions, with social partners involved in the process.
 The parties also plan to work together next year on a medium-term, formula-based agreement. Its aim would be to ensure that nominal wage increases reflect the country’s economic performance while remaining fair to employees.
